newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Southern bluefin tuna faces "commercial extinction.
newsitem.headline: Southern bluefin tuna faces "commercial extinction.

text.p: Southern bluefin tuna, the primary catch for the luxury Japanese sashimi trade, faces "commercial extinction" due to overfishing, says a World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) report released on Wednesday.
The report says mature southern bluefin tuna stock was below the level considered safe for the species' survival and probably would not remain economically viable to fish.
"There is no doubt that the decline in the population of southern bluefin tuna has been severe and that the situation with the parental biomass is now critical," the report says.

"The collapse of significant fisheries in the past several decades has indicated that it is possible to fish marine species to commercial extinction. If the warning signs are ignored, this possibility exists for the southern bluefin tuna."
The WWF report says the current annual catch of the fish was 11,750 tonnes, compared with a peak of 81,000 tonnes in 1961, with prices for individual fish fetching more than US$60,000.
It said a 35 percent reduction in the annual catch was necessary to replenish breeding stocks to safe levels by 2020.

"The status of the southern bluefin tuna parental population is now less than nine percent of that in 1960," said Glenn Sant, a senior research officer with TRAFFIC Oceania, a wildlife trade monitoring organisation, who assisted in compiling the report.
"Given the serious implications that a collapse in the stock would have on the species, ecosystem and fishing industry, we need to adopt a precautionary approach," Sant said.
The WWF said Australia annually exported around A$47 million (US$35 million) worth of southern bluefin tuna to Japan and accounted for one quarter of the global catch.

The report called on Australia, Japan and New Zealand -- the main southern bluefin tuna fishing nations -- to cut the catch at next month's meeting in Australia of the Commission of the Convention for the Conservation of Southern Bluefin Tuna.

"Current conservation efforts are greatly undermined by Japan's import of southern bluefin tuna from nations which are not party to the convention," Sant said. "Japan should suspend this practice until these nations join the convention."

The report said increasing catches by Taiwan, Indonesia and Korea, who are not part of the convention, were threatening tuna stocks by targeting breeding grounds off the coast of Java. (A$1 = US$0.74)
